period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: Hearing and Chanting the Poem Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Recite (p.103): read aloud and recite the poem together.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the full poem aloud twice at a natural pace, pointing to the text as she reads. Students follow along in their textbooks (p.103), tracking each line.
Let us Recite ("first whole-class choral recitation of the poem"). Teacher leads stanza by stanza, students echo after each stanza, then the class recites all three stanzas together.

Pairs take turns reciting a stanza each to their partner while the partner listens and gives a thumbs-up when the rhythm sounds right. Teacher circulates and models the swing-like rise and fall of the lines.
Three volunteers each recite one stanza to the class; teacher invites a brief whole-class response on which line felt most like swinging and why.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's rhyme scheme (ABAB) and the repeated phrase 'Up in the air' carry its swinging rhythm — help children feel that rhythm physically by swaying gently as they chant rather than reading it in a flat monotone. Students who find individual recitation daunting can stay with the choral voice; the goal at this point is confident, joyful familiarity with the whole poem.

periods.activity_title: Listening for Rhymes and Sharing Swing Experiences

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.107): listen to the poem and list rhyming word pairs.
Let us Think B (p.104): discuss personal swing experiences and imagined views.

time_bands.activity: Teacher tells students they are about to listen carefully for rhyming pairs and asks them to keep a small slip of paper ready to jot words as they hear them.

Let us Listen ("listening for rhyming pairs in the poem"). Teacher reads the poem aloud three times at a moderate pace. After each reading, students call out pairs they caught; teacher lists them on the board (swing–thing, blue–do, wall–all, wide–countryside, green–seen, brown–down).
Students add two rhyming pairs of their own choice to their slips and share with a partner, then several pairs are shared with the class and discussed briefly.

Let us Think B ("discussing personal swing experiences and imagined aerial views"). Students share in pairs: where they have seen a swing and what it was made of. Then each student tells the class one thing they would love to see if they were up in the air on a swing.

Teacher brings the discussion to a gentle close by connecting students' imagined views to the countryside images in the poem — rivers, trees, cattle — asking which image from the poem they liked most.

periods.teacher_notes: Having chanted the poem together, students now listen with a focused purpose — finding sound patterns rather than just enjoying the ride. The discussion questions are open-ended; accept all reasonable imagined views and resist correcting students toward the poem's images; the goal is genuine oral participation.
materials: Small paper slips for jotting words

periods.activity_title: Reading the Poem Closely and Discussing Comprehension

tasks_in_class.task_brief: New Words (p.103–104): read and understand pleasantest, cattle, countryside.
Let us Think A (p.104): answer questions about what the poet sees and feels.

time_bands.activity: Teacher does a short shared reading of the poem (p.103), pausing at 'pleasantest', 'cattle', and 'countryside' each time they appear. For each word, teacher elicits meaning through context — 'What kind of word might describe something a child thinks is the best?' — before confirming the meaning.

New Words ("read and work out the meanings of pleasantest, cattle, countryside"). Students read the three words aloud, use them in a simple spoken sentence each, and teacher writes a short context phrase on the board for each.

Let us Think A ("whole-class comprehension discussion: what the poet sees, which lines show enjoyment, and why the air is called blue"). Teacher reads each question aloud; students think silently for a moment, then share with a partner before a whole-class discussion is held, with teacher scribing key phrases on the board.

Students write their responses to all three questions in their notebooks independently, using the board phrases as a scaffold. Teacher moves around to read drafts and offer a quick word of confirmation or a guiding question.

periods.teacher_notes: The third question — 'Why do you think the poet says the air is blue?' — invites interpretive thinking, not a single right answer; accept 'blue sky', 'open air', and imaginative responses equally. The poem's appreciation centres on the joy of ascending and the wide view it offers, so guide discussion toward images of height and freedom rather than asking children to name poetic devices by term.

periods.activity_title: Words That Work Two Ways — Verbs and Nouns

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen — Verbs and Nouns (pp.105–106): identify verb and noun uses of the same word in sentence pairs.

homework.task_brief: Let us Speak (p.107): practise the /W/ tongue twister and word list at home, making an 'O' shape with the lips for each /W/ sound.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'I swing on a swing' on the board and asks students which word appears twice. Through guided questioning, students identify that the first 'swing' is doing something (verb) and the second 'swing' is a thing (noun). Teacher introduces the idea that some words can work as both.

Let us Listen — Verbs and Nouns ("circle the verb, underline the noun across sentence pairs for dance, play, answer"). Teacher reads each sentence pair aloud; students circle or underline in their textbooks (pp.105–106) and then the class discusses each pair, with teacher confirming on the board.

Students continue independently with the sentence pairs for 'fly' and 'waves' (p.106), then compare answers with a neighbour. Teacher leads a brief whole-class check, asking students to read the sentence that shows the word as a verb and the one that shows it as a noun.

Quick consolidation: teacher asks students to say one original sentence using any of the five words as a noun, and another using the same word as a verb. Several students share their pairs aloud; class confirms whether each use is noun or verb.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem itself supplies the anchor: 'swing' as a verb (the action of swinging) and as a noun (the object) makes the concept concrete before the textbook examples begin. When students circle and underline, circulate to check that they are looking at the function in the sentence, not just guessing by position — 'play' as a noun comes after 'watch a', which is a useful clue to highlight.

periods.activity_title: Sentence Expansion — Making Every Sentence Longer

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn (p.104): expand sentences step by step, each new sentence longer than the last.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes a bare sentence on the board — 'The child swings.' — and asks students to add one detail. She accepts suggestions and builds the sentence live: 'The child swings high.' → 'The child swings high in the park.' Discuss what kind of information was added each time (where, when, why, how).

Let us Learn ("model the Jeevan example and discuss how each expansion adds new information"). Teacher reads the Jeevan example (p.104) aloud, pointing to what was added at each step. Students identify the expansion type (place, time, reason) for each new step.

Students work in pairs to write their own expanding set, starting from a short sentence of their choice and writing at least four steps. Teacher moves around, prompting pairs who are stuck with questions like 'Where did this happen?' or 'Why did she do that?'.

Three or four pairs read their expanding chains aloud; class listens and calls out what kind of detail was added at each step. Teacher closes by noting that skilled writers add information in exactly this way to make their sentences more precise and interesting.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with fixed sentence pairs in the verb–noun activity, students now build sentences freely — a different kind of word work that asks them to think about meaning and detail rather than grammatical category. Watch for students who simply repeat the last sentence with one word changed; prompt them to add a genuinely new piece of information at each step.

periods.activity_title: Writing About What I Enjoy and Using Prepositions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write 1 (p.108): write a short paragraph about activities enjoyed in free time.
Let us Write 2 (p.109): fill in prepositions for a garden scene picture.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects the poem's word 'pleasantest' to the idea of things we find most enjoyable, asks three students to name one free-time activity each, and lists them on the board to show that there are many kinds of enjoyable activities.

Let us Write 1 ("guided paragraph: activities I enjoy in my free time"). Teacher models a two-sentence opening on the board: 'In my free time I love ___. I also enjoy ___ because ___.' Students draft their own paragraph in their notebooks, using the model as a scaffold. Teacher circulates, reads drafts, and offers a single improvement suggestion to each student.
Two students read their paragraphs aloud; class listens and one peer volunteer says one thing they liked about the paragraph. Brief, positive tone throughout.

Let us Write 2 ("preposition fill-in for the garden picture on p.109"). Teacher directs students to the illustration, names the items visible (ladybug, butterfly, honeybee, watercan, ant, caterpillar, leaf) and the preposition box. Students look at the picture carefully and complete all seven blanks, then compare with a partner.

periods.teacher_notes: The two writing tasks in this unit differ in nature — the paragraph is open and expressive while the preposition exercise is closed and picture-driven; keep the energy distinct so students experience both as useful rather than as one long writing block. For the preposition exercise, the picture on p.109 is the essential reference; encourage students to trace with a finger the spatial relationship before choosing a word rather than guessing from memory.

periods.activity_title: Imagining a Magical Swing — Drawing, Writing and Sharing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.110): draw a magical swing and write a short paragraph about the adventure.

homework.task_brief: Let us Explore (p.110): find out which festivals or months are linked with swinging on swings and note two facts to share.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to imagine: 'If your swing could take you anywhere at all — outer space, a jungle, inside a storybook — where would you go?' Students whisper their answer to a neighbour. Teacher takes three quick shares to warm up the imagination.

Let us Do ("draw the magical swing and its destination"). Students draw their magical swing scene on a blank page in their notebooks or on a sheet of paper. Teacher encourages bold colour and detail — what does the sky look like there? What is on the ground below?

Let us Do ("write a short paragraph about the adventure the magical swing brings"). Using their drawing as a plan, students write three to five sentences describing where the swing took them and what they saw or did. Teacher circulates and prompts with 'What happened first? What surprised you?'

Three or four students hold up their drawings and read their adventure paragraphs aloud. Class listens and one volunteer says one vivid detail they heard. Teacher closes by reminding students that Stevenson's poem began the same way — with a child imagining what the swing might show — and their own swings of imagination carry that spirit forward.

periods.teacher_notes: Having written a paragraph about real free-time activities earlier, students now write imaginative prose prompted by their own drawing — a richer creative demand that is supported rather than repeated. Students who finish drawing quickly should move directly to writing; the drawing is a planning tool, not a finished art product, so brief sketches are entirely appropriate.

items.source_context: Poem by Robert Louis Stevenson; imagery of swinging, countryside views, pleasantest, cattle, blue air.
items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 103 beginning "Rivers and trees and cattle and all". What does the poet see when the swing carries him over the wall? Choose the correct answer.

options.label: A
options.text: Rivers, trees, cattle, and the wide countryside

options.label: B
options.text: A brown roof and a green garden only

options.label: C
options.text: The inside of his own house and backyard

options.label: D
options.text: A busy market and tall buildings

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have conflated the third stanza's garden and roof images with the over-the-wall view in the second stanza.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student likely read 'over the wall' as looking inward rather than outward into the countryside.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student is not drawing on the poem's rural imagery and may be importing a familiar urban setting.

items.source_context: Poem by Robert Louis Stevenson; imagery of swinging, countryside views, pleasantest, cattle, blue air.
items.item_stem: The poet calls swinging "the pleasantest thing / Ever a child can do." Do you think he really enjoys it? Write one or two sentences explaining what in the poem makes you think so.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Yes, the poet clearly enjoys swinging. He says it is the pleasantest thing a child can do, and he describes flying up into the blue air and seeing rivers, trees, and cattle, showing great delight in the experience.

items.source_context: Rhyming pairs in 'The Swing'; personal swing experiences; imagined aerial views from the poem.
items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the poem aloud (page 103). Listen carefully. Which pair of words from the poem rhyme with each other?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True: 'swing' and 'thing' end with the same sound. 2 — False: 'wall' rhymes with 'all', not 'wide'. 3 — True: 'green' and 'seen' share the same ending sound. 4 — False: 'blue' rhymes with 'do', and 'brown' rhymes with 'down'.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are on a swing that goes very high — higher than in the poem. What three things would you see below you or around you? Tell your partner in two or three sentences.

expected_elements: Names at least two specific things seen from height.
Speaks in connected sentences, not single words.
Uses at least one direction word (above, below, over, across).
